summary: William Henry Coxe was a linguistics and Indology scholar who studied Classics and Sanskrit at Balliol College, Oxford (1858). He served as an Assistant at the British Museum (1861–1865) and held posts with the Indian Education Service and King's College London in 1865.
William Henry Fox Talbot worked in the field of history and archaeology. He was educated at Harrow School until 1815 and subsequently studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, from 1817 to 1821.

William Henry Hale was an Indology and linguistics scholar. He studied at Yale University, earning a B.A. (~1856–1860) and Ph.D. (~1860–1863), and completed an LL.B. at Albany Law School (~1860–1861).

William Henry Harris worked in philosophy and religious studies. Educated at Southern Nazarene University (B.A.), Boston University (Ph.D.), and under T. M. P. Mahadevan at the University of Madras (1953–1954), he taught at the University of Arkansas and Southern Illinois University Edwardsville.

William Henry Mill was an Indology and religious studies scholar who earned degrees at Trinity College and the University of Cambridge. He served as Principal of Bishop's College, Calcutta (~1820–1838), and later became Cambridge's Christian Advocate (1840) and Regius Professor of Hebrew (1848).

William Henry Sleeman worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He served in the Bengal Army (1809–1854), rising to Major-General, and held posts with the East India Company (1820), the Thuggee and Dacoity Department (1835), and as Resident at the University of Lucknow (1849–1856).

William Henry Sykes was an Indology, history, and archaeology scholar. He founded the Asiatic Society of Mumbai and served as President of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland in 1858.

William Henry Wait was a linguistics and Indology scholar. He studied at Northwestern University, Allegheny College (Ph.D., 1888), Berlin, and Bonn. After teaching at Illinois Wesleyan University, he served at the University of Michigan from 1895 to 1925.

William Hoey worked in Indology, history, and archaeology. After earning an M.A. at Queen's University Belfast (~1865–1869), he served as Reader in Hindustani and Indian History at the University of Oxford (~1906–1919) and Trinity College Dublin (1910).

William Holme Williams was an Indology and linguistics scholar. After graduating from the University of Wisconsin-Madison (A.B., 1876), he spent his career there as an instructor and professor of Greek, Hebrew, Sanskrit, and Semitic languages between 1879 and 1917.
William Homan Thorpe studied at Jesus College, Cambridge (~1921–1925). He later held an academic post at the University of Cambridge from circa 1932 to 1969, where he taught John Hurrell Crook.

William Hook Morley worked in Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and history/archaeology. Called to the bar at the Middle Temple in 1840, he later served as a member (1847) and Librarian (1859) of the Royal Asiatic Society.

William Howard Campbell was a linguistics and Indology scholar. He completed an M.A. and B.D. at the University of Edinburgh (~1878–1882) and subsequently served as a missionary with the London Missionary Society from 1884 to 1903.
William Hoyles Drew was an Indologist who studied under the traditional teacher Ramanujan. He served with the London Missionary Society as chaplain of the Madras Chapel from 1834 to 1856.

William Hunter was an Indology and linguistics scholar who studied at Marischal College and the University of Aberdeen (M.A., ~1773–1777). He served the East India Company, the Agra Residency, The Asiatic Society (1798–1811), and Fort William College (1805–1811).
William Irvine was a scholar in history, archaeology, and Indology. He studied at King's College London (~1861–1862) and served as a civil servant in the Indian Civil Service from 1864 to 1888.

Linguist William J. Gedney studied at Whitman College and Yale University under Franklin Edgerton. He held posts at Cornell University (1955), the University of Ceylon (1959–1960), and as Professor of Linguistics at the University of Michigan (1960–1981).

William James was a philosopher and religious studies scholar who studied at Plymouth College and Harvard University, including Harvard Medical School. He held various faculty positions at Harvard from 1872, becoming professor in 1885, and taught students including George Santayana.

William Jones was an Indologist and linguist educated at Harrow, Oxford, and the Middle Temple. He served as a judge in Fort William and Calcutta, and founded The Asiatic Society in 1784 while studying under Indian traditional scholars.

William Joseph Wilkins was an Indology and religious studies scholar educated at Highgate School and Hackney College (~1868–1870). From circa 1870 to 1884, he taught at Bhownipur College and the Bhowanipore Missionary Institution for the London Missionary Society.
